title: 13 — Checklists & Interview Q&A

13 — Checklists & Interview Q&A

The consolidated layer: a production-readiness checklist you can run through before a launch, and ~50 CI/CD and Azure interview questions at the 3–5 year bar.

PART A — Checklists

A1. Production readiness (run through this before go-live)

Identity & security

  • Managed identity on every compute resource — and on every deployment slot
  • Zero connection strings containing keys; storage account keys disabled
  • Data-plane RBAC roles granted (not just Contributor)
  • Key Vault: RBAC authorisation, purge protection, private endpoint + DNS zone
  • Secrets referenced via Key Vault references or App Configuration; none in source, images, or logs
  • TLS 1.2+, HTTPS only, FTPS disabled
  • Private endpoints for data services, with the privatelink DNS zones linked
  • Defender for Cloud enabled; no unaddressed high-severity recommendations
  • API authorisation deny-by-default, checked server-side per resource

Reliability

  • ≥2 instances, zone redundant
  • Health checks: /health/live and /health/ready, readiness not hard-failing on shared dependencies
  • Graceful shutdown with a drain window
  • Timeouts, jittered retries (idempotent only), and circuit breakers on every external call
  • Transient-fault retry enabled for Azure SQL
  • Backups configured and a restore tested; RPO/RTO documented
  • Failover plan documented and, ideally, rehearsed
  • Load tested at 2× expected peak; the failure mode past the ceiling is known

Delivery

  • Pipeline in the repo; build once, promote the artifact
  • Immutable tags (git SHA); no latest
  • OIDC/workload identity federation — no stored cloud credentials in CI
  • Production deployment requires an approval, recorded
  • Deploy → warm up → smoke test → swap → verify → auto-rollback on failure
  • Migrations as a separate idempotent step, backward compatible for one version
  • Rollback path proven, not theoretical

Operability

  • Application Insights connected; cloud_RoleName set
  • Correlation ID through every log, span, and message — including across queues
  • Dashboards: service, business, deep-dive, with deployment markers
  • Alerts on symptoms with runbooks and owners; DLQ, cert expiry, and Service Health alerts configured
  • Log volume and cost reviewed; sampling configured
  • Runbook for the top five alerts
  • On-call rota and escalation path defined

Cost

  • Right-sized from measured usage, not from fear
  • Tags applied for owner, environment, and cost centre
  • Budget with alerts at 50/80/100%; anomaly detection on
  • Lifecycle policies on storage; non-prod auto-shutdown outside working hours

A2. Pipeline review checklist

  • PR feedback under ~10 minutes
  • Static analysis, unit tests, secret scan, and dependency scan all blocking
  • Integration tests against real infrastructure (Testcontainers), not in-memory fakes
  • Coverage gated on changed lines not decreasing; zero known-flaky blocking tests
  • Third-party actions/tasks pinned to a SHA; least-privilege job permissions
  • Separate credentials per environment, scoped to a resource group
  • Shared logic in reusable workflows/templates, referenced by tag
  • Concurrency configured: cancel on PRs, queue on deploys
  • Artifacts and caches have deliberate retention

A3. The ten most common Azure mistakes

# Mistake Fix
1 Contributor granted, app still gets 403 Grant the data-plane role (Storage Blob Data Contributor, Key Vault Secrets User…)
2 Private endpoint with no private DNS zone Link the privatelink.* zone to the VNet
3 Deployment slot missing its own RBAC Each slot has its own managed identity — grant it
4 Connection string points at the wrong environment after a swap Mark environment-specific settings as slot settings
5 Single instance, no Always On, no slots in production ≥2 instances, Always On, staging slot
6 new HttpClient() / new SDK client per request Register SDK clients as singletons
7 Function scaling to 200 instances and killing the database maxConcurrentCalls + functionAppScaleLimit matched to downstream capacity
8 Auto-migrate on startup with multiple instances Migrations as a separate pipeline step
9 Cosmos partition key chosen without thought High cardinality, even distribution, in the dominant query, <20 GB per logical partition — and immutable
10 Application Insights bill exploding Sampling, per-table retention, and fixing the one chatty log line

PART B — Interview Q&A

B1. CI/CD (15 questions)

Q1. What's the difference between continuous integration, delivery, and deployment? CI: every change is merged frequently and automatically built and tested. Continuous delivery: every change that passes CI is deployable at any time via a push-button release. Continuous deployment: it's released automatically with no human gate. Most teams do CI plus manual-approval delivery — say which you actually do; an inflated answer invites a follow-up you can't defend.

Q2. Why "build once, promote the artifact"? If you rebuild per environment, production runs bits that were never tested — a different restore, base image digest, or transitive dependency. Building once also makes rollback trivial (redeploy the previous tag) and makes "what's in production?" answerable. Configuration is injected at runtime, never baked in.

Q3. How do you deploy a breaking database change with zero downtime? Expand → migrate → contract, across three releases. Add the new nullable column, deploy code that writes both, backfill in batches, switch reads, deploy, and only then drop the old column. The middle release must work with both schemas — that's what makes rollback possible. Skipping this is why teams say "we can't roll back, the migration already ran."

Q4. How should a pipeline authenticate to Azure? Workload identity federation / OIDC. The runner requests a short-lived token describing the workflow; Azure matches its iss and sub claims against a federated credential on an app registration or user-assigned managed identity and issues an Azure token. No secret to expire, rotate, or leak. Bind the subject to a GitHub Environment (or a specific Azure DevOps service connection) so approvals gate credential issuance.

Q5. Compare deployment strategies. Rolling (default for stateless, no downtime, gradual rollback); blue/green (2× infra, instant rollback — App Service slots are blue/green); canary (gradual exposure gated on metrics); feature flags (deploy dark, release by toggle in seconds — the highest-leverage practice, and it composes with all the others). All of them require backward-compatible changes.

Q6. Your deployment broke production. What do you do in the next ten minutes? Assess user impact and blast radius → mitigate first (swap the slot back, redeploy the previous tag, toggle the flag off) → then diagnose using what-changed, traces, and logs → blameless postmortem with a systemic fix. Mitigate before diagnose is the point: users don't care about root cause.

Q7. How do you keep a pipeline fast? Parallelise independent jobs, cache dependencies with a lockfile-derived key, split test suites by stage (unit on PR, integration on merge, E2E nightly), path-filter in a monorepo, fail fast with the cheapest checks first, and right-size the runners — developer waiting time usually costs more than a bigger runner.

Q8. What's wrong with secrets in CI variables? They're a standing leak surface, need rotation, and are visible to anyone who can edit the pipeline (they can echo a transformed version). Use OIDC to the cloud, managed identity between resources, and a vault for the rest. If one leaks: rotate first, then investigate, then clean history.

Q9. Why pin third-party actions to a commit SHA? Tags are mutable. A compromised action running under a mutable tag executes with access to everything in the job, including its secrets. Pin the SHA and let Dependabot bump it.

Q10. What's dangerous about pull_request_target? It runs with write permissions and repository secrets in the base-repo context. Checking out and executing the fork's code hands an attacker your secrets. It's a well-known critical vulnerability pattern.

Q11. job vs deployment job in Azure DevOps? A deployment job targets an environment, which gives you approvals and checks, per-environment deployment history, automatic artifact download, and deployment strategies with routeTraffic, postRouteTraffic, and on.failure hooks — the built-in place for verify-then-rollback.

Q12. ${{ }} vs $[ ] vs $( ) in Azure Pipelines? Compile-time template expansion / runtime expression evaluated before the job starts / runtime variable used inside a step. Using ${{ }} where you need a runtime value is a very common bug.

Q13. How do you enforce that every pipeline runs a security scan? Azure DevOps: required (extends) templates at the organisation level, so teams cannot bypass them with their own YAML. GitHub: organisation-level required workflows plus branch protection requiring the named status checks.

Q14. What metrics tell you a delivery process is healthy? DORA: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore. Plus pipeline duration p50/p95, pipeline success rate, and flaky-test rate. Not lines of code or "automation coverage" — those measure activity and are trivially gamed.

Q15. Trunk-based or GitFlow? GitHub Flow (short-lived branches + PR) with feature flags for most teams; trunk-based if the team has the test discipline for it. GitFlow suits versioned products with multiple supported releases and is a poor fit for continuous delivery to a single web environment — the long-lived branches produce exactly the integration pain CI exists to remove.

B2. Azure platform (12 questions)

Q16. Subscription vs resource group? Subscription = billing and quota boundary (⚠️ quotas are per subscription per region). Resource group = lifecycle and management boundary — deleting it deletes everything inside. Group by application + environment, not by resource type, so you can deploy and delete an application cleanly.

Q17. Explain the control plane / data plane distinction in RBAC. Control plane = managing the resource (ARM operations). Data plane = accessing the data in it. Contributor on a storage account lets you change its tier and read its keys, but does not grant Storage Blob Data Contributor, which is what code needs to read a blob with Entra auth. This is the most common Azure 403 and the reason people wrongly fall back to access keys.

Q18. System-assigned vs user-assigned managed identity? System-assigned lives and dies with the resource; user-assigned is independent and shareable. Prefer user-assigned under IaC because the principal ID stays stable — a recreated resource with a system-assigned identity gets a new principal ID and every role assignment breaks.

Q19. How does a managed identity actually get a token? The platform exposes the Instance Metadata Service on a link-local address (169.254.169.254); the SDK requests a token for the target resource and caches it. That's also why SSRF in Azure is dangerous — a request forgery reaching IMDS can steal the app's identity token.

Q20. What is DefaultAzureCredential? A credential chain: environment variables → workload identity → managed identity → Visual Studio → Azure CLI → interactive browser. The same code authenticates as your developer identity locally and as a managed identity in Azure, with no configuration difference and no secrets. In production, exclude the developer credentials to cut startup latency and remove ambiguity.

Q21. How do you deploy infrastructure safely? IaC (Bicep/Terraform) in the repo, what-if/plan output in the PR as the review artifact, apply on merge, no manual portal changes, incremental deployment mode, and deterministic guid() names for role assignments so the deployment is idempotent. ⚠️ Never output a secret — deployment outputs are readable in the deployment history.

Q22. Zone redundancy vs region pairs? Availability zones are physically separate datacentres within a region — zone-redundant deployment survives a datacentre failure at modest cost, and should be the production default. Region pairs are for geo-replication and staged platform updates; multi-region is a 10× complexity step because you have to solve data consistency, so only do it when the business pays for it.

Q23. My app can't reach Azure SQL over a private endpoint. Why? Almost always DNS. The FQDN must resolve to the private IP, which requires the privatelink.database.windows.net private DNS zone linked to the VNet, plus the app resolving through Azure DNS and having VNet integration for outbound traffic. Symptom: works from a VM in the VNet, times out from App Service.

Q24. A partner has allow-listed our App Service outbound IP and calls started failing. Why? App Service outbound IPs can change when you scale or change tier. Put a NAT Gateway with a static public IP in front and give the partner that.

Q25. How do you control Azure costs? Right-size from metrics; reservations or savings plans for the steady baseline; auto-shutdown non-production; storage lifecycle policies; tune Log Analytics retention and sampling (frequently a top-3 line item); watch egress; tag everything and review cost by tag monthly; budgets with anomaly alerts. The classic surprises are telemetry ingestion, a Cosmos container left at load-test RUs, and orphaned public IPs or disks.

Q26. What are the five Well-Architected pillars? Reliability, Security, Cost optimisation, Operational excellence, Performance efficiency. Useful because it's the shared vocabulary in Azure architecture reviews.

Q27. How would you enforce governance across many subscriptions? Management groups for scope, Azure Policy for enforcement (required tags, allowed regions, deny public blob access, require HTTPS), initiatives for benchmark bundles, PIM for just-in-time admin access, and Defender for Cloud for posture. Resource locks on production data resources — noting a lock also blocks your IaC pipeline.

B3. Azure services (20 questions)

Q28. App Service, Container Apps, Functions, or AKS? Standard web app or API → App Service (slots, simplicity). Containerised with event-driven or scale-to-zero needs → Container Apps (KEDA, revisions, Dapr). Event-driven/scheduled short work → Functions. Many services with complex networking and a platform team → AKS. Count what AKS gives you versus the operational work it adds; if it's fewer, don't.

Q29. How do you achieve zero-downtime deployment on App Service, and what actually happens in a swap? Deploy to a staging slot, warm it up, verify health, swap, verify production, and swap back to roll back. The swap applies production's sticky settings to staging, restarts staging with them, warms it up by sending HTTP requests to the warm-up path, then flips the load-balancer routing. The old version stays in staging as your instant rollback.

Q30. Which settings swap and which stay with the slot? Anything marked "deployment slot setting" stays — environment-specific app settings and connection strings, custom domains, TLS bindings, scale settings, and the managed identity (each slot has its own). Everything else follows the code. ⚠️ The classic bug is a staging connection string that isn't marked sticky, so production ends up pointed at the staging database after a swap.

Q31. Why is ARR affinity usually wrong? It pins users to instances with a cookie, unbalancing load and complicating draining and deployment. It also hides the real problem — in-process state. Turn it off and move session/cache state out.

Q32. What breaks when you scale App Service from 1 to 5 instances? In-memory cache and session; in-process schedulers now running five times; SignalR without a backplane; local file writes; in-process locks. Each needs to move to a distributed equivalent or leader election.

Q33. In-process vs isolated worker for .NET Azure Functions? Isolated runs your code in a separate process with full Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting DI and middleware, any .NET version, and no assembly conflicts with the host. The in-process model is retired on 10 November 2026 (as is .NET 8 support), and it isn't supported on Flex Consumption at all — so isolated on .NET 10 is the destination.

Q34. Consumption vs Premium vs Flex Consumption? Consumption: scale to zero, cold starts, limited VNet. Premium: pre-warmed instances, full VNet, no scale to zero, expensive at idle. Flex Consumption: scale to zero with always-ready instances and full VNet — the modern default for Linux, and required for .NET 10 on Linux since classic Linux Consumption is being retired.

Q35. My Function isn't triggering at all and there are no errors. Where do you look? AzureWebJobsStorage. The runtime uses it for triggers, leases, checkpoints, and timer schedules. If it's misconfigured or the identity lacks the blob/queue/table data roles, functions silently never fire. It's the single most common cause.

Q36. A queue-triggered Function is overwhelming the database. What do you do? Cap maxConcurrentCalls in host.json and set functionAppScaleLimit, matched to the downstream connection capacity — and make sure clients are injected singletons rather than created per invocation. Instances × concurrency is the real parallelism number.

Q37. Why must Function handlers be idempotent? Delivery is at-least-once. A message can be redelivered after a lock expiry, a host restart mid-processing, or a retry. Idempotency via a dedupe key committed in the same transaction as the effect — or a naturally idempotent operation — is the only real protection.

Q38. What can't you do in a Durable Functions orchestrator? Anything non-deterministic. The orchestrator is replayed from its event history, so no DateTime.UtcNow (use context.CurrentUtcDateTime), no Guid.NewGuid() (use context.NewGuid()), no randomness, no I/O — put all of that in activity functions.

Q39. Service Bus vs Event Grid vs Event Hubs vs Storage Queue? Service Bus: reliable discrete business messages with ordering (sessions), transactions, scheduling, and dead-lettering. Event Grid: push-based reactive event routing with fan-out and retries. Event Hubs: high-throughput replayable streams partitioned for parallel consumption. Storage Queue: cheap and simple, with none of the guarantees. A good combined pattern is Event Grid routing into a Service Bus queue for reliable processing.

Q40. Explain peek-lock and its main failure mode. The message is locked rather than deleted until you Complete it. If processing outlasts the lock (default 30s), the broker redelivers it while you're still working — so you get duplicate processing. Defences: renew the lock, keep handlers short, and be idempotent. The last one is the only guarantee.

Q41. How do you guarantee ordering while still scaling consumers? Service Bus sessions keyed by entity id: ordered within a session, parallel across sessions. Then name the costs — a hot session becomes a bottleneck, and a repeatedly-failing message stalls the whole session. The alternative is making the consumer order-insensitive with a version number on the entity.

Q42. How do you reliably write to the database and publish a message? Transactional outbox: write the business change and an outbox row in one transaction; a relay publishes and marks them sent. Or CDC off the transaction log. Never dual-write. It gives at-least-once publishing, which is why consumers must be idempotent.

Q43. How would you let a browser upload a 1 GB file? Issue a short-lived, write-only user-delegation SAS and have the client upload directly to Blob Storage; the API only mints the URL and records metadata on confirmation. Proxying the bytes through App Service consumes memory, threads, and request-timeout budget for no benefit.

Q44. Account key vs SAS vs Entra ID for storage? Account keys grant full control and can't be scoped or attributed — disable them (allowSharedKeyAccess: false). SAS is scoped and time-limited, but a service SAS is still key-derived; a user-delegation SAS is signed with an Entra credential so it's revocable and attributable. Entra ID with managed identity is the default for service-to-service.

Q45. Why did my app get 403 on Key Vault after I gave it Contributor? Contributor is control plane. Reading a secret needs Key Vault Secrets User on the data plane, with enableRbacAuthorization: true. And if it's a deployment slot, remember the slot has its own identity.

Q46. How do you rotate a secret with zero downtime? Design for two valid credentials during an overlap: generate the new one at the source, store it as a new Key Vault version, let applications pick it up (Key Vault reference refresh, App Configuration sentinel key, or a restart/swap), verify nothing uses the old one, then revoke it. Two-key services (Storage, Cosmos, Service Bus, Redis) make this trivial. The best strategy is having no secret at all — managed identity.

Q47. Key Vault or App Configuration? Key Vault for secrets; App Configuration for non-secret settings and feature flags. App Configuration is far cheaper to read frequently, supports labels for per-environment values, has built-in dynamic refresh via a sentinel key, and can hold Key Vault references — so you get one configuration surface with secrets resolved transparently.

Q48. How do you choose a Cosmos DB partition key? High cardinality, even distribution of both storage and request volume, present in your dominant query (or every query is a cross-partition scan), and keeping each logical partition under 20 GB. It's immutable after creation, so getting it wrong means a data migration. Synthetic or hierarchical keys when no single property works.

Q49. Why is transient-fault retry mandatory on Azure SQL? It's a multi-tenant PaaS — failovers, maintenance, and throttling drop connections routinely. EnableRetryOnFailure turns invisible maintenance into invisible maintenance; without it, it becomes a user-visible incident. ⚠️ And with it enabled, manual transactions must be wrapped in the execution strategy.

Q50. What breaks if Redis goes down? If the answer isn't "we degrade to the database and stay up", the cache is an availability dependency rather than an optimisation — and the origin must be capacity-planned for a cold cache. Also: register IConnectionMultiplexer as a singleton, set allkeys-lru eviction, give every key a TTL, and never use KEYS in production.

B4. Scenario questions

S1. "Design the deployment pipeline for a .NET API and Angular SPA going to Azure." Cover, in this order: trigger and branching model → parallel build jobs (backend, frontend, security scan) → build once with an immutable SHA tag → artifact published → OIDC authentication to Azure → migrations as a separate idempotent step → deploy to a staging slot → warm-up and smoke test → swap → verify → auto-rollback on failure → production gated by an environment approval → observability and DORA metrics. Mention reusable workflows/templates for the second service onward.

S2. "Our releases cause five minutes of errors every time. Fix it." Diagnose: is it cold start (no warm-up, no Always On), missing readiness gating, in-flight requests killed (no graceful shutdown), or a non-backward-compatible migration? Fix: staging slot with a warm-up path that primes dependencies, Always On, health-check-gated swap, terminationGracePeriod/ShutdownTimeout longer than the longest request, expand/migrate/contract for schema changes, and a post-swap verification that swaps back on failure.

S3. "We have secrets in 40 places. Give me a plan." Inventory and classify first (what, where, who uses it, can it be federated?). Then: enable secret scanning in CI and pre-commit to stop the bleeding → replace anything that supports it with managed identity (SQL, Storage, Service Bus, Cosmos, Key Vault) → move pipeline credentials to OIDC federation → put the genuinely irreducible third-party keys in Key Vault, surfaced via Key Vault references → set expiry dates and rotation alerts → rotate everything that was ever committed. Sequence it by blast radius: production credentials first.

S4. "The application is slow. It's Azure's fault." Establish the facts before the blame: is it one endpoint, one region, or everything; did it start at a deploy; what do p95/p99 say versus the average. Then walk the trace — DB, downstream HTTP, CPU, or waiting. Check Azure Service Health for a genuine platform incident. The common real causes: an N+1 or missing index, sync-over-async causing thread-pool starvation, a cold cache, a connection pool exhausted, or a tier hitting its throttling ceiling (check sys.dm_db_resource_stats before blaming the query).

S5. "How would you make this single-region app survive a regional outage?" First ask what the business will pay for, and what RTO/RPO they actually need — the honest answer is often that zone redundancy plus tested backups is sufficient. If genuine multi-region is required: active-passive with a failover group for SQL (stable listener endpoint), geo-replicated storage, Front Door for traffic steering, infrastructure deployed from the same IaC to both regions, and — the hard part — a documented, rehearsed failover runbook. Active-active means solving cross-region data consistency, which is a different order of complexity.

Final revision list

If you remember only fifteen things from this whole set:

  1. Build once, promote the artifact; configuration is injected.
  2. OIDC federation for pipelines; managed identity for workloads. Zero stored secrets.
  3. Control plane ≠ data plane — grant the data role.
  4. Every slot has its own managed identity.
  5. Expand → migrate → contract, always.
  6. Deploy to a slot, warm it up, verify, swap, verify, swap back.
  7. Private endpoint without private DNS = mysterious timeout.
  8. SDK clients are singletons. Always.
  9. At-least-once delivery ⇒ idempotent consumers.
  10. Transactional outbox, never a dual write.
  11. Cosmos partition keys are immutable — choose as if you can't change it, because you can't.
  12. Azure SQL will drop your connections; enable retry.
  13. Alert on symptoms, not causes; every alert needs a runbook and an owner.
  14. Correlation IDs everywhere, including across queues.
  15. A backup you haven't restored is a hypothesis.
